messages.subject: RE: WAIC's a go
parts:
Hi Bob,

I'm following up on an old conversation you posted on the development mailing list, regarding saving log likelihoods for WAIC.

From your post I understand that ll_y should save the log-likelihoods for each data point for each sample:

generated quantities {
     double ll_y[N,T];

     for (n in 1:N)
       for (t in 1:T)
         ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);
   }

Shouldn't it be:

ll_y[n,t] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);

instead of:

ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);

I'm asking because I tried something equivalent and the extracted ll_y array was all 0's whereas using the ll_y[N,T] version yet wasn't when I used the ll_y[n,t] version.

Does this make sense?


Thanks,

rubi

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RE: WAIC's a go
parts:
On 5/1/13 6:07 PM, rubi wrote:

> I'm following up on an old conversation you posted on the development mailing list, regarding saving log likelihoods for
> WAIC.
>
> From your post I understand that ll_y should save the log-likelihoods for each data point for each sample:
>
> generated quantities {
> double ll_y[N,T];
>
> for (n in 1:N)
> for (t in 1:T)
> ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);
> }
>
> Shouldn't it be:
>
> ll_y[n,t] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);
>
> instead of:
>
> ll_y[N,T] <- normal_log(alpha[n] + beta[n] * (x[t] - xbar),sigma_y);

Absolutely. The former will only set one entry.
Sorry for the buggy example.

You want to look at the formulas for computed p_{WAIC 1}
and "computed p_{WAIC 2}" in the paper Andrew linked (by
Andrew, Jessica Hwang and Aki Vehtari):

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf

Note that unlike DIC, you don't need to evaluate the log
probability at the posterior mean. But you still can't
evaluate the formula fully within Stan, because you need
averages across samples. But it should be pretty easy in R.

Note that Andrew has a habit of renaming things. "WAIC" was
called the "widely applicable information criteria" by
Watanabe.

If you get an example working, it'd be great if you could post
it back to the list.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RE: WAIC's a go
parts:
I have a very simple working example of computing WAIC from Stan samples. I did it entirely in R, though, to avoid having to store all those likelihoods in the Stan output. I'll go ahead and attach the script, in case it dispels some confusion for someone. (The script is very didactic, using loops and redundancy to make the algorithm more transparent. It could definitely be refactored for speed.)

The formula I used is the p_{WAIC 2} on page 8 of Gelman, Hwang, & Vehtari. 

I also have an experimental module for glmer2stan that computes WAIC. I haven't put it up on github yet, as I'm not sure I understand WAIC yet, and also I'm not sure how to deal with WAIC in zero-inflated models. But this functionality will appear before long. The strategy I've taken, again, is to do everything outside of Stan, saving on storage. I have some Stan models with 20k parameters and 14k data points, and I doubt saving the likelihoods in Stan is going to be a sane approach there.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] WAIC's a go
parts:
The downside of computing the per-data-point likelihoods
in either Stan's generated quantities block or in R is
that you have to duplicate information that's in the model.
The problem in general with doing this in R is that I don't think
all of the parameterizations of distributions match. (We should
really have a table for this in our doc.)

What we'd really like to do, but haven't quite figured out how to do,
is do all of this automatically based on the model specification.
What I envision is something like this in a very very simple case:

model {
prior {
mu ~ normal(0,10);
sigma ~ uniform(0,100);
}
likelihood {
for (n in 1:N)

y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma); // save these quantities
}
}

so that we could figure out the likelihoods here.
Then we could potentially monitor these as we go and
calculate running totals using something like Welford's
algorithm.

The reason this isn't so easy is that Stan allows all
kinds of things other than simple sampling statements in
the code. In general, the likelihood might require side
calculations, local variables, etc. which are hard to tease
apart from the relevant amounts.

The alternative that Andrew's been suggesting would be
to somehow annotate the regular code, so it'd look more
like:

model {
mu ~ normal(0,10);
sigma ~ uniform(0,100);
for (n in 1:N)

y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma); @likelihood
}

where the annotation @likelihood indicates that
the likelihood for a variableis being defined. Another
way of doing this would be something like this:

model {
...
for (n in 1:N) {
real ll;
for (n in 1:N) {
ll <- normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma);
for_waic(y[n],ll); // store likelihood for WAIC
lp__ <- lp__ + ll;
}
}

Any of these approaches bring up all kinds of issues
where things can go wrong. For instance, if there's an
if/else statement, you have to make sure each variable gets
its likelihood in every block.

- Bob

For example, if this is my model:

Yij ~ N(µj,σj)       //observation i of group j, both mean and variance are unknown

σj ~ HalfCauchy(γ) //γ would either be an empirical value or a hyperparameter distributed γ ~ U(0,∞)

Thanks a lot,
rubi

> in either Stan's generated quantities block or in R is
> that you have to duplicate information that's in the model.
> The problem in general with doing this in R is that I don't think
> all of the parameterizations of distributions match. (We should
> really have a table for this in our doc.)
>
> What we'd really like to do, but haven't quite figured out how to do,
> is do all of this automatically based on the model specification.
> What I envision is something like this in a very very simple case:
>
> model {
> prior {
> mu ~ normal(0,10);
> sigma ~ uniform(0,100);
> }
> likelihood {
> for (n in 1:N)
> y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma); // save these quantities
> }
> }
>
> so that we could figure out the likelihoods here.
> Then we could potentially monitor these as we go and
> calculate running totals using something like Welford's
> algorithm.

> The reason this isn't so easy is that Stan allows all
> kinds of things other than simple sampling statements in
> the code. In general, the likelihood might require side
> calculations, local variables, etc. which are hard to tease
> apart from the relevant amounts.
